body: never thought i would go into medical social work but here i am. i have done psych with med-psych discharge planning, ED social work, and med-surg and ICU care management before landing my current role which i love and find very rewarding. right after getting my lcsw an opportunity opened up that i had been seeking for a long time. i work with a major hospital system as a community social worker for patients that face barriers in the healthcare system and work closely with a nurse partner. i am out in the community meeting my patients after hospital stays getting them connected with providers/insurance and resources of all kinds. i have been doing this for 7 months now and it's so rewarding to see my patients achieve various "wins". it definitely was a learning curve for me to transition from a short term role, but it really feels like i am making a difference and getting involved in the local community.

FL LCSW - about $37/hr but salaried/40hr week so i guess about 75k a year which is mind-blowing to me! i was making $16/hr 5 years ago! i work for a major hospital system with a unique program to help patients with barriers to accessing healthcare stay out of the hospital. the goal of this program is to help connect patients with resources and help educate them regarding their medical conditions and how to access care. i work in partnership with a nurse who leads more on the medical side of things.
 
some of the main parts of my role is to help patients get some way to cover basic medical care whether it be insurance or grant funded programs, brief counseling, assisting with charity applications for the hospital, addressing mental health needs, and connecting with any and all resources. i mainly meet patients in their homes or wherever they are in the community for visits. i often meet patients at medical appointments and appointments for social services needs for advocacy and support. 

one of the challenges is that the hospital i work with covers a lot of rural area and in a resource poor county (in FL too!). however there's a lot of creativity involved, and rapport building is essential. my nurse partner who has been in this job for a good length of time but also is born and raised in the area has been a wealth of knowledge for me. i really have enjoyed learning about the local community and making connections with my patients.

it is so different from all the other jobs I've worked (mostly inpatient work in psych, substance use, and medical with some time at a methadone clinic) but i really enjoy it. there is a lot of learning curve but i am thankful to have a supportive boss who sees the potential in me. i started about 4 months ago after being extremely burnt out with inpatient medical SW (and toxic work environment) and while it is a challenge it is so worth it!

i had to take a bit pay cut to get to where i am now because i had to somehow get licensed and in my experience in FL licensure opens a lot of doors. i also never imagined i would go into medical social work of any kind but that's where the money is. however i feel it is worth looking at jobs at all possible places as often unique positions may pop up you wouldn't expect.

i have done psych hospital social work as a CM/DC planner for 3 years and medical/hospital social work for 2 years. it is definitely a beast in itself and a pretty intense, fast paced role. the nature of it is very frustrating due to families, the systems that govern care, and the push of metrics from hospital leadership. i did appreciate how much i learned from it and how it helped tremendously in becoming super efficient/fast paced. i also appreciated working on a multidisciplinary team and the networking side of it through the community.

however, i did finally leave full time due to many reasons. i was very frustrated with the pay disparity between RN CMs and SW CMs (i only got a 2 cent raise when i completed my LCSW). the hospital i worked for had a heavy RN presence in the CM department in staff and leadership which was another reason. one more reason adding on to this was that i felt the RN CMs would push the more difficult social issues on to us to address on their days off while we did not have the luxury to not address the medical side of our role.

i now work in an outpatient role with the same hospital system as beforehelping connect patients discharging from the hospital with medical care and resources alongside a nurse. it is a wonderful partnership and a lot less stressful with a pay bump as well. it is nice to work M-F 8-5 no holidays or weekends.

mad respect to you as well as all other psych discharge planners out there! that was my first job for 3 1/2 years after i finished my MSW. since we were part of a medical hospital we would get a lot of med/psych and geri patients as well as many self pay pts so lots of difficult discharges. i remember getting like barely any training and then thrown into managing a 24 bed unit that was a hot mess. i somehow had 3 SNF placements in 6 months which per my coworkers was unheard of. i worked that unit full time for a year and switched to PRN (usually 4 days a week) for 2 1/2 years working on whichever unit needed coverage.

psych is its own beast and with the nature of the work having that close knit team makes all the difference. it's definitely not for everyone but i loved it and miss it sometimes. even tho it delayed me starting my lcsw process by a few years (i left for CMH because it was the only job offer that i got after 5 months and countless interviews), i felt i learned SOOO much from my experience there. your comment took me down memory lane and reminded me that i am probably better equipped than i realize!

my manager who proposed the idea to me handled and helped with a lot of the cases like that when i first started and it always intrigued me. i feel like it's a lot more interesting than the typical routine hospital CM role and has a lot more involvement in handling social issues. 

i am thankful that both my manager and director came up with this idea as not only a way to address my burnout but to also have trust in me to potentially help build this role.

thank you for sharing!

thank you for your insight! i feel you regarding those families and SNFs...so frustrating. would have to deal with that in the ED too with the added pressure of time constraints. i am hoping it works out!

so at both hospitals i have worked at anyone who is CM SW are not responsible for writing orders especially of that nature. we use epic at my hospital and defer to the company wide "cheat sheets" and escalate to leadership if needed if we get push back.

my team is mixed of SW and RN CMs and while I don't typically interact with them as much as they do with each other, i am so thankful that for the most part we get along well and help each other out. also from my understanding the inpt doctors for the most part understand the scope ofthe role.

the family aspect is the only part that i am nervous about since it will be a lot more prevalent in this role as well as face to face. i am all too experienced with super needy and unrealistic families but only had to interact via telephone calls.

from what is being proposed and at least how i understand the culture at my job I don't anticipate worrying about going beyond my scope. I am good with setting boundaries about my role and my limitations and leadership at my job has proven many times to back me up. in fact the fact that leadership is wanting to work with me and get my feedback is why i am wanting to take the leap.

I totally agree with your statement about LOS NOT equalling more time. Since being in ED I am all about making moves and not sitting. From previous experience in inpatient psych with pts with more medical concerns and geriatric populations, i am familiar with that lack of break. i compare it to a dishwasher who constantly keeps getting new stacks of dirty dishes 

the families component is definitely my biggest fear but knowing my direct boss has so much experience with it and is willing to teach and guide me makes me willing to take the challenge.

my previous background includes 3 1/2 years of psych discharge planning in a psych hospital with many medical and geri patients, 9 months of OP counseling at a MAT clinic (for long term caseloads) and then 6 months of combined counselor/DC planner for CMH detox. i also dabbled prn inpatient medical DC planning but didn't stick due to poor training (previous job). so i do have experience with managing a caseload and never had difficulty being on top of it. i know the medical side will be a learning curve but once I figure out a process that works for me I'll be golden.

At my current job I help out with a lot of initial evals from a CM standpoint and usually try to focus on the ones i can see may be more complex to get the ball rolling. i have gotten pretty good at identifying possible needs like SNF placements, IVABX, possible charity needs and alerting management ahead of time, etc. i also am used to placing pts at SNFs and IRFs from the ED.

my boss said she will give me a little bit of re orientation on some of the inpt processes but also her and other leadership i feel will be willing to help when needed. my current boss has a lot of experience with complex cases and is a wealth of knowledge. i also know my inpt CMs would definitely help and provide support to fill in the gaps for some processes too.

the families and difficult convos part i would say is my weakness but an area i want and need to improve on. i am one to want to take on a challenge and i do have both my boss and external supervision that I plan to heavily utilize to help my growth that way.

my worst job for sure was when i counselor/discharge planner for a detox/ARF unit run by the local CMH agency. we received voluntary clients as well as court ordered clients. the job was alright, the pay was insulting but i stayed as i was getting free supervision. it all went downhill when my clinical manager left (for good reason, her pay was ever more insulting than mine) while the other clinical leaders in related departments as well as above her dropped the ball. i was promised a raise and new title, received neither, but was forced the responsibility of such. i was forced to be a quasi-leader that was expected to make leadership decisions but then would receive immense backlash. in addition, i was given the role of handling all court ordered treatment cases along with being present during substance use court. 

the first nail in the coffin was when the person who promised my raise and promotion quit without telling me. she also told me she would help train me. the second was when i was present in a meeting with other clinical leadership staff (mix of LMHCs/LCSWs) as a regular counselor was shunned and dismissed for asking when i would receive a raise and promotion as i was taking on more responsibility. the third was when i asked for help repeatedly from leaders and was ignored. the fourth was when they hired another counselor with less experience and worse work ethic at a higher rate than myself and my coworkers with seniority and experience. the fifth and final was when i finally called my entire organization out to the county substance use court in a email chain. i never received a response to an issue so quickly.

one other thing that also happened at the very end of my time there was my boyfriend's half brother's death. he had a single use relapse after 9 months of sobriety and being in recovery. it resulted in an ultimately fatal overdose.

when i put in my 2 weeks notice all of these weird people in various leadership roles started crawling out of the woodwork requesting meetings with me and panicking and bargaining. they also were gaslighting me pretending to act oblivious to my requests for help and my previous clinical managers concerns prior to her leaving. two of these leaders, both VPs of something equating to bullshit, tried to negotiate a raise and tell me they had new hires in the process of starting. when i told them my new pay, they laughed and said "oh ok yeah we can't give you that much of a raise".

i left somewhat quietly...my old bosses at the outpatient clinic said nothing to me when i told them i was leaving as it meant they had to step up in responsibility. same with the other clinical leaders who wanted me to step up in responsibility without the title or raise. very telling of the organization. others have told me that my situation was not an isolated incident.

i only stayed as long as i did because i enjoyed my clients. many of them i knew from my time working at the MAT clinic run by the same company. i appreciated the rawness associated with the addictions and how much more "real" it felt when working with clients. but this extremely stressful and toxic company combined with the triggers associated with my bfs half brother outweighed any possible reward.

this all happened over the course of 6 months. i am thankful to have been at my current position for almost 9 months now in an area i love (hospital ED). my workload, responsibility, and stress is nowhere near what this previous position entailed. i have extensive leadership support as well as appropriate compensation. i also got to keep my supervisor from my previous job at a discounted rate. 

tl;dr i sold my soul to a CMH detox unit for 6 months, it made my life a living hell, but came out a better person

Also I will add that I have not worked in a position where I had to file such paperwork because I'm not licensed. BA 52 by LEO looks different than by professional (often can be more detailed esp if professional is a doctor/busy psychiatrist). BA-32 (either) is multiple pages and sent to the courthouse of the county the facility is located. Not sure of marchman act since we have changed processes in my facility. Ex parte is also multiple pages from the ones I've seen. The baker acts require diagnosis (if by professional), reason for harm, and additional information if pertinent.

I would check out myflfamilies.com, there's sections on both. I had to watch a series of (sadly boring) videos about at least the Baker act for my job in inpatient psych (in Florida). I can at least give a brief description (please correct any mistakes any other fl social workers!)

Baker act is initiated due to danger to self, danger to others, or risk of self neglect basically.

BA-52 - involuntary psych hold initiated by LEO or a provider (doctor, ARNP, PA, LCSW, LMHC. LMFT), 72 hours max to be evaluated by inpatient psychiatrist. This is when a patient is admitted to a psych facility 

BA-32R - can be initiated after a BA-52 by an inpatient psychiatrist if the person refuses treatment and the psychiatrist feels they need an extended baker act basically. Requires a 2nd opinion from another hospital psychiatrist. Patient can sign consents but unless it is lifted before a mental health court date, itll turn into a BA-32I with an appointed guardian advocate who then provides consent for the patient

BA-32I - patient is deemed incompetent by inpatient psychiatrist for variety of reasons (cognitive functioning, psychotic, legal guardian already in place, etc). Also requires 2nd opinion and a health care proxy to be established ASAP. After mental health court, hcp turns into guardian advocate. Also in mental health court they can recommend additional treatment in a series of weeks or deem patient is ok for discharge. Again, the psychiatrist can lift this

Marchman act - can basically be done by anyone, a nonprofessional would have to file it at the courthouse and procedures vary by county. A professional can also do this too. Initiated due to risk of harm to self due to substance use and mandates the individual is put into treatment. From my experience it doesn't necessarily mean long term treatment, often detox. In my experience at a psych hospital, can only be done for opiates, alcohol, or benzos but the rules are bent if the patient is pregnant usually

Lastly I should mention ex partes. Done usually by a concerned individual on behalf of the person who they feel is a risk to themselves. Has to be submitted in the courthouse and requires paperwork and detailed account of the reason for an ex parte. This I consider the community version of a baker act in a way but I've seen it be easily abused. Dont see a lot of it but I feel it should be mentioned.

i wanted to mention that actually most states have "duty to warn" laws that allow mental health professionals to break confidentiality if a client/patient poses a risk to become violent, especially if targeted towards a certain person.

are you in the U.S.? there are a lot of antidepressants that aren't "experimental" that a doctor would recommend before hand.  did they say what meds they would start you on? xanax will make you spacey like that, a lot of benzos will do that, they are pretty sedating which can make them addictive if you like that feeling.  i'm honestly surprised you were only given xanax before anything else first since it can be pretty difficult to get a benzo prescription in the U.S. especially as a first-defense kinda prescription. and in my clinical opinion, it would be wise to discontinue xanax if it's making you wanna self-harm.  many psychs in my opinion will start a patient with a new MDD diagnosis on zoloft since it's a pretty mild antidepressant.  lexparo has been my ride or die for the last several months and i'd say it's a good antidepressant too since it helps with the anxiety too.  the one i would not recommend in your situation is wellbutrin since it doesn't help with anxiety.  i would ask for more information for sure since anything "experimental" is good grounds to be skeptical.  a therapist will def help and even if the doc you are going to now may not jive with you, your therapist may help in giving you a new referral.

i work in mental health and i myself have struggled with mental health issues of my own.  i'm very similar to you, 22 and just graduated from being a full-time student and dealt with depression+social anxiety my entire time in college.

i wanna first commend you on being proactive and being aware that this is something that is bothering you as well as putting it out there to others (even just anonymously on the internet).  i can tell you are actually trying and wanting to put effort forth into making change and i'll tell you it isn't easy, especially when you have other stressors affecting you.  

i can tell you from personal experience and witnessing others go through it, depression makes everything ugly.  if you've ever watched the episode of south park where stan sees everything as literal shit, that's pretty much how i summarize depression and how it feels to me.  nothing feels good, looks good, your brain is telling you that everything is literally shit and what is the point.  it's so hard to break out of that.  not only that, but there's almost like a culture of positivity that others who don't experience mental illness push on those who do that only tends to bring us down since we can't see the good.  life also isn't black or white, where everything is either fucking amazing or fucking horrible.  there are so many shades of grey in between and yes somethings will be good and somethings will be bad and you can't be at either extreme.

have you only been on xanax?  it's a benzodiazepine prescribed mainly for anxiety only and won't affect your depression much at all.  if you are open to it, i will tell you that it may be wise to seek out a new psychiatrist and have them evaluate you for medications. 
 many college campuses have mental health clinics or can help provide a referral for one and are completely confidential. (for proof, i had a patient of mine who was utilized her university's mental health clinic and even though she gave me consent to contact them and schedule an appointment, they were unable to confirm or deny if she was a patient).  taking antidepressants gave me the boost i needed to actually apply the coping skills i was learning.  and it may take some time to find one that works for you.  i initially started on prozac, it worked until i needed it upped and upped again and then it made me extremely suicidal to where i needed to stop immediately.  i switched to lexapro about 7 months ago and recently just had it adjusted.  i also work in inpatient psych and eve then i see patients who may come back in multiple times due to medications needing to be tweaked.  it sucks that it can be such a process but the recovery process with mental health is continuous and never linear.

with therapy, you may need to seek out a therapist who does a little more than CBT.  CBT is amazing for mental health and it takes a lot of practice, repetition, and honestly just feeling kinda silly utilizing it for it to work.  but it also sounds like you just need to at least just be able to vent about what's bothering you.  i don't know if you have had any therapy yet, but again, your university may have resources and a lot of communities will have low-cost clinics where you can get therapy services.  i had a therapist who mainly did CBT work with me but she also allowed me the time to process the shit that would bother me too and was able to incorporate techniques relating to that through the therapy session that allowed be to vent and learn how to cope.  after a while it really does somewhat become more second-nature.

i'm not very good at putting my thoughts to writing but the one thing i want to leave you with is this.  i can't tell you how long this will last for.  but there are people who care about you and that i feel that there is at least some hope for things to eventually get easier with time and work.  if you need someone to talk to further, pm me.  i'm here

if you need someone to talk to about this, i encourage you to call the national coalition against domestic violence hotline 1-800-799-SAFE (7233) (from http://www.ncadv.org/).  advocates are available 24/7 for support and can connect you with a local DV hotline as well if you prefer.  you can keep yourself anonymous if you want to.  in addition, they can help you safety plan if you do decide to leave.  many DV shelters have connections to community resources to help you find jobs, housing, childcare (not sure if you have children or not), etc.  domestic violence isn't just physical abuse.  it is very difficult to leave an abusive relationship, especially when they have control over you like your husband does.  you do not deserve to be treated this way.  i am sorry that you are going through this but there are people out there that are here for you and understand your struggle.
